title: Subhuti asks (section 2)
hook: how should one set out on the bodhisattva path, and hold the mind?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Diamond Sutra opened on an ordinary morning: robe, bowl, alms, a meal, washed feet, a seat. Your line: an ordinary morning.

The Buddha has just sat down. The monks have settled around him. The grove is quiet. Somebody has to go first. Classrooms know this moment: the teacher is ready, the room is full, and nobody wants to be the one to break the silence with a question that might sound foolish. In the Diamond Sutra, one monk stands up. He's an elder, and his name is Subhuti. What he asks is the question the whole sutra will spend itself answering.
screen: `THE ROOM IS QUIET.` → `SOMEBODY HAS TO GO FIRST.` → `ONE MONK STANDS.`

segments.voice: First, how he asks. The sutra slows down to show it. Subhuti rises from his place in the assembly, arranges his upper robe over one shoulder, kneels on his right knee, joins his palms toward the Buddha, and bows. The body asks before the mouth does. Second, what he says first. Not his question. He begins with wonder: how much the bodhisattvas have been helped, he says, how much they've been cared for by the Tathagata. Before he asks for anything, he notices what's already been given. Third, the question itself. Paraphrased: when someone has set out on the bodhisattva path, how should they stand? How should they go on? And how should they hold the mind? Three parts, really one: where do I put my feet, how do I keep walking, and what do I do with this restless thing behind my eyes? It's a beginner's question, and Subhuti is no beginner. That's part of its force: the elder asks it on behalf of everyone who's just starting. Fourth, the answer that isn't one yet. The Buddha says, well said, Subhuti, well said. Listen, and take it well to heart, and I'll tell you. And Subhuti says, so be it, and waits. That's the whole of section two: the question asked, praised, and left hanging in the air overnight. Some readers find a teaching there too: a good question deserves a moment of silence before anyone rushes to answer it.
screen: `THE BODY ASKS FIRST.` · `WONDER BEFORE THE QUESTION.` · `HOW TO STAND, GO, HOLD THE MIND.` · `WELL SAID. LISTEN.` · then, large: `HOW TO HOLD THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Sit up a little, the way Subhuti knelt, with some care in how you hold yourself. Then ask, in your own words, the question under your questions right now: not the to-do list, the one underneath. Don't answer it; ask it once, clearly, and let it hang in the quiet, the way his did.
Subhuti. The elder monk who rises, kneels, and asks the Diamond Sutra's question: how to stand, how to go on, how to hold the mind. Today's word.
Your line: how to hold the mind. A good question can wait overnight. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1119 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: ALL BEINGS FREED, NONE FREED (SECTION 3).`

howItsDone: In monasteries that follow this custom, a monk who asks a teacher a question in assembly rises, arranges the robe over one shoulder, kneels and joins palms, as Subhuti does in the Diamond Sutra; the sutra itself is chanted and studied in Mahayana communities.
